paragraphs.heading: Second layer up
paragraphs.text: The stratosphere is the second layer of Earth's atmosphere counting from the ground, above the troposphere and beneath the mesosphere. Its name comes from the Ancient Greek word for a layer or stratum. Where it begins depends on where you are: about 20 km up near the equator, around 10 km at mid-latitudes and about 7 km at the poles.

paragraphs.heading: Warmer as you climb
paragraphs.text: In the troposphere below, air cools with height, but the stratosphere gets warmer the higher you go, a reversal called a temperature inversion. The cause is the ozone layer, which absorbs ultraviolet (UV) light from the Sun. Average temperatures run from −51 °C near the tropopause, its lower border, to −15 °C near the mesosphere. The very top, called the stratopause, sits at about 270 K (−3 °C), and above it temperature falls with height.

paragraphs.heading: How ozone heats the air
paragraphs.text: In 1930 the British scientist Sydney Chapman described how the ozone layer forms, a process now called the Chapman cycle. Oxygen molecules (O₂) absorb high-energy UV-C sunlight with wavelengths shorter than about 240 nm and split apart. The freed oxygen atoms join other O₂ molecules to make ozone (O₃). Sunlight breaks ozone much faster than it breaks O₂, giving O and O₂, and the loose atom joins O₂ to rebuild ozone while releasing heat. This rapid breaking and rebuilding is what warms the stratosphere.

paragraphs.heading: Calm, dry and layered
paragraphs.text: With warmer air sitting on cooler air, the stratosphere resists being stirred up and down, which is why it is layered. There is no regular convection here, and none of the turbulence that comes with it. Only very energetic events, such as volcanic eruption columns or the tops of severe thunderstorms, push convection into it, and only briefly and locally. All air entering it must cross the tropopause, a temperature minimum, and is freeze-dried on the way, so the stratosphere is very dry.

paragraphs.heading: Where planes fly
paragraphs.text: Airliners usually cruise at 9 to 12 km, which in temperate latitudes puts them in the lowest part of the stratosphere. The low temperatures and thin air there reduce drag on the airframe and save fuel. Flying this high also keeps them above the turbulent weather of the troposphere. Some aircraft cruised higher still: Concorde flew at Mach 2 at about 18 km, and the SR-71 at Mach 3 at about 26 km.

paragraphs.heading: Winds and circulation
paragraphs.text: Winds here can far outpace those of the troposphere, nearing 60 m/s in the Southern polar vortex. The overall flow is called the Brewer-Dobson circulation, a single loop in which air rises out of the tropical troposphere and sinks outside the tropics. In roughly half of northern hemisphere winters, the stratosphere goes through a sudden warming, caused by the absorption of waves known as Rossby waves.
